content: Individuals or organizations that received substantial funding from private entities, particularly pharmaceutical companies, or researchers and clinicians who were paid honoraria exceeding $5,000 by pharmaceutical companies, were deemed to have a conflict of interest. Consequently, their involvement in the Guidelines Development Group (GDG) was classified as restricted. Members of the GDG with restricted participation included Charles Gore, Francesco Negro, Jurgen Rockstroh, and Alexander Thompson. These individuals contributed to the development of PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions and provided technical expertise in reviewing evidence summaries. However, they were excluded from discussions, voting, and the formulation of recommendations (refer to Annex 1, page 80). The declarations of interest forms submitted by members of the External Review Group were reviewed in accordance with the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines development policy. Any identified conflicts of interest were taken into account when interpreting comments from these members during the external review process. Notably, external reviewers were not permitted to make changes to the recommendations (refer to Annex 2, page 83). Dissemination and Updating of Guidelines The Global Hepatitis Programme Secretariat will distribute the guidelines through WHO regional offices to country offices and Ministries of Health. Additionally, the guidelines will be shared with key international, regional, and national collaborating centers, civil society organizations, and national programs. The guidelines will also be accessible on the WHO website, with links to other United Nations and related websites. The successful implementation of these recommendations will depend on a well-planned and appropriate process of adaptation and integration into relevant regional and national strategies. This process will be influenced by available resources, existing enabling policies and practices, and the level of support from partner agencies, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and civil society. To monitor policy uptake, the Global Hepatitis Programme (GHP) conducted a country profile survey in 2016/2017. Regarding the care cascade, GHP has established a monitoring and evaluation framework and generated initial estimates for 2015 and 2016. In 2018, GHP plans to implement a new system of routine reporting to obtain annual updates on these indicators. This system will be instrumental in assessing the impact of the guidelines at the country level. The GDG acknowledged that the field of hepatitis treatment is rapidly evolving. New data on the treatment of hepatitis C virus (HCV)-infected adolescents and children are expected in the coming years, necessitating an update to the guidelines by 2020. Evidence Informing the Recommendations Systematic reviews, meta-analyses, modeling, cost-effectiveness analyses, values and preferences assessments, and feasibility surveys were conducted to support the formulation of recommendations and identify patient-important outcomes. Existing national and international guidelines were also evaluated. Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses For the recommendation to treat all individuals diagnosed with HCV infection, WHO commissioned a systematic review and meta-analysis of morbidity and mortality from extrahepatic manifestations in HCV-infected individuals. For updated recommendations on treatment with direct-acting antivirals (DAAs), a systematic review was conducted. Manufacturers of relevant DAAs (AbbVie and Gilead) were contacted to provide additional clinical trial data. Observational cohort studies and data from Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) treatment programs in South Africa and Cambodia were also considered. Modeling Modeling was performed to predict the impact of HCV treatment on the incidence of new infections. National and subnational models were used to estimate the prevention impact of treating a fixed number of HCV infections in various regions (refer to Web Annex 4). Feasibility Survey An online feasibility survey assessed programmatic and personal experiences with implementing a Treat All recommendation. The survey, distributed to members of the GDG and their networks, was completed by 10 program managers, 145 healthcare providers, and 112 individuals living with HCV. The questionnaire focused on experiences, perceived challenges, and suggested solutions for implementing a Treat All approach (refer to Web Annex 7). Cost-Effectiveness Analyses WHO commissioned a systematic review of cost-effectiveness literature to evaluate the economic and population health outcomes of a Treat All scenario compared to more restricted access policies. Values and Preferences A stakeholder survey and literature review were conducted to determine which treatment characteristics are most important from a patient perspective. Among 112 individuals living with HCV who responded to the WHO survey, nearly all supported a Treat All policy and advocated for universal access to treatment. However, 18% expressed concerns about the acceptability of treatment among individuals without fibrosis or with mild fibrosis, highlighting the need for careful messaging to convey the benefits of early treatment. Summary of Evidence Treating HCV infection benefits all infected individuals. DAAs, available since 2013, achieve high sustained virological response (SVR) rates, generally exceeding 90%, except in individuals with advanced cirrhosis or HCV genotype 3. Achieving SVR is associated with reduced liver-related mortality, lower risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and improved extrahepatic manifestations. A 2017 meta-analysis showed that individuals with SVR had an 87% reduction in liver-related mortality, an 80% reduction in HCC incidence, and a 75% reduction in all-cause mortality compared to those without SVR. DAA treatment is highly effective and well-tolerated in adolescents. It has also been reported to improve cognitive functioning, educational attainment, and overall well-being. Treating all HCV-infected individuals modestly reduces transmission risk, with prevention benefits varying across countries and regions. Factors influencing the number of infections averted include population growth rates and the prevalence of HCV among people who inject drugs (PWID). Recommendations WHO recommends offering treatment to all individuals aged 12 years and older diagnosed with HCV infection, regardless of disease stage, except for pregnant women. This strong recommendation is based on moderate-quality evidence. Implementation Considerations Transitioning to a Treat All approach requires careful planning, particularly in settings with limited resources. Integration of treatment for PWID with harm reduction services is essential to prevent reinfections. In settings with high HCV prevalence among PWID, concurrent investments in harm reduction programs are critical to enhance the cost-effectiveness of treatment. Research Gaps Further research is needed on long-term clinical outcomes of early-stage HCV treatment with DAAs, post-marketing surveillance for adverse events and drug resistance, cost-effectiveness studies in diverse settings, and the impact of expanded DAA treatment on HCV incidence, particularly in high-risk populations such as PWID and men who have sex with men (MSM).
